text: Ugarit is unusually useful for a Late Bronze Age simulation because archives preserve administration, diplomacy, literature, religion, economy, and multiple scripts/languages.
Ugarit had a cosmopolitan scribal environment using alphabetic Ugaritic cuneiform alongside Akkadian and contact with multiple other languages/scripts.
limitations: Does not imply broad population literacy.

text: Urban households at Ugarit were materially unequal; house sizes and access to wells varied, and many wells were private.
limitations: Archaeological access patterns do not by themselves reveal complete household rights.

text: Patrilocal joint-family arrangements have been proposed for parts of Ugarit, but households should not be assumed uniform.
limitations: Model as competing/partial household arrangements, not default destiny.

text: Household religion at Ugarit can plausibly involve health, safe childbirth, prosperity, weather, crops, livestock, and family continuity.
limitations: Ordinary personal belief remains unevenly visible.

text: Ugarit was a maritime-commercial hinge where agriculture, merchants, palace interests, and international exchange overlapped.
limitations: Do not infer a total palace command economy.

text: Households, kin obligations, property, patronage, and local reputation often constrained individual choice in documented Bronze Age settings.
limitations: Strength and form vary by place/status/time.

text: Religion and practical action overlapped; ritual/divination can be part of decision-making under uncertainty rather than decorative behavior.
limitations: Specific beliefs and specialist access are local.

text: Information can be delayed, distorted, intercepted, mistranslated, or superseded by events.
limitations: Exact delays depend on route and messenger.

text: A civilization label cannot support a population personality distribution; culture should constrain structures and expectations instead.
